body: Before applying, I read the four stores the way the posting describes the job: fairhavenhealth.com in full and bariatricfusion.com, vitalnutrients.co and unjury.com sampled — 397 published products, 57 page fetches, no logins. The review, with working fixes and a weekly QA workbook, is at mousabatarseh.com/blueroot-review/. It opens with what works, and a lot does: Fairhaven scores 95 of 100 on the 29-check rubric I run on Michigan storefronts, the best result I have measured this year.

The findings are the operating gaps a Monday checklist catches. Three of the eight footer "Shop" links open an empty or one-sold-out-item collection. Because All Products sorts A–Z, the one sold-out product sits second on the page and second in the search drawer's Trending Now on every page of the store. Five single-variant products carry a "30% off select sizes" badge while the card, the PDP, the JSON-LD and the subscription price all show full price. Every one of 20 sampled titles runs 73–91 characters. And the four stores ship from one address with three free-shipping thresholds and two delivery promises. Each finding on the page has a count, the Shopify change that fixes it, and a working prototype built on your own product data.

For seven years I have run retail and wholesale storefronts on Shopify and WooCommerce: product setup and catalog data for 14,000+ SKUs, promotions and seasonal launches, the QA that keeps prices and pages honest, and the GA4 and Search Console reporting behind it. The weekly sheet on the page is the cadence I would run from the first Monday.

Two things to say plainly. I have not administered Recharge, and my 3PL coordination has been with a warehouse rather than a named fulfillment partner — the order flow, inventory sync and exception handling are the same work. I stayed away from all health and product-claim language; that review belongs to your regulatory team.
cover.closing: I'd welcome a call to walk through the review and the workbook.

body: The posting asks for a résumé and a brief summary of experience. Here is the summary, and something more useful: before applying I read royalapparel.net the way the job describes it — the sitemap's 1,063 URLs, the Men's category, 20 product pages and the dataLayer on every template, no logins, no carts. The review, with working fixes, is at mousabatarseh.com/royal-apparel-review/. It opens with what works: fresh hero merchandising dated within the last three weeks, 28 colors and 107 photos on style 5051, wholesale terms stated precisely, and a search that puts a style number in position one.

The data around the garments is where the coordinator's work is. No page on the site carries a canonical tag, and four hostname variants answer 200 with the same body. The sitemap is 38% redirecting CGI links and lists the cart, login and checkout templates; three of twenty sampled products are dead or obsolete and still return 200. Every product page carries the same five-star rating from 326 reviews, with availability left blank. The GA4 impressions on the Men's category have empty item names and brands, so the reporting the posting asks for can't attribute what merchandising does. Each finding on the page has a count, a fix written at the template or server level, and a prototype built on your own product data — including the category grid re-rendered server-side and the single Product schema your feeds need.

For seven years I merchandised and ran wholesale and retail storefronts for two textile and apparel brands: styles, colors and sizes for 14,000+ SKUs, coupons and the seasonal promo calendar, banners and Mailchimp assets, product data for wholesale accounts, and the technical SEO and GA4 reporting underneath. Blank apparel is the catalog I know best.

Two things to say plainly. I have supported paid search and social rather than owned them, and I have not worked in Faire, Sage or ASI directly — the product-data side of those feeds is the same work as the marketplace and wholesale exports I have run. I am in Michigan and glad to work remote, or hybrid on a schedule that suits Hauppauge.
cover.closing: I'd welcome a call to walk through the review.

cover.re: Re: Full Stack IT Specialist, E-Commerce Developer & Content Editor (Plymouth, MI)
body: Before applying, I read federalfp.com the way the posting describes the job: three of the nine sitemap files (54,496 URLs), five category pages, 19 product pages and eight content pages, plus five on patriothyd.com — no logins, no carts, no quote requests. The review, with working fixes built on your own catalog, is at mousabatarseh.com/federal-fluid-power-review/. It opens with what works: part-number search returns the right part, the product pages carry Product, Offer, shipping and breadcrumb schema most distributors never ship, and the Engineering Toolbox is real content.

The catalog behind it shows the marks of a bulk ERP import that nobody has mapped yet. 20,242 product URLs (37% of what I read) have no URL key, so the sitemap sends Google twenty thousand pages your own robots.txt blocks. Thread size, port, material and pressure live inside title strings — none of the 19 sampled product pages has them as attributes — and where attributes exist, the Cylinders filters hold twins like 2.5 and 2.5", and two values are Excel date serials (44628 is 3/8). Nine of nineteen products are Request Pricing, yet print a price and declare InStock. Supplier logos stand in for photos on 69% of the catalog. Every page shares one meta description, and Federal's footer still reads "© 2023 Patriot Hydraulics" with Patriot's phone number in the header. Each finding on the page has a count, the Magento setting or import that fixes it, and a working tool: a URL-key generator, an attribute parser you can paste any product name into, an option normalizer, and a meta-template preview across the sample.

For seven years I have run wholesale and retail catalogs and the sites in front of them: 14,000+ SKUs maintained by bulk CSV, migrations with redirects intact, data mapped between an inventory system and the store, WordPress and WooCommerce administration, HTML, CSS and JavaScript, and Python for the scripts that clean data before it is imported. I'm in Warren, 35 minutes from Plymouth, and on-site is fine.

Two things to say plainly. My platform years are WooCommerce and Shopify rather than Magento — the attribute sets, import model and URL rewrites are the same shape, and the fixes on the page are written for Magento's admin. And I can cover the internal IT and network support the posting lists as a secondary duty, but I would want to be honest that the catalog work is where I am strongest.
cover.closing: I'd welcome a call, or a visit to Plymouth, to walk through the review.
